## 1. Setup and How to Use This Notebook {#guide-1}

This Quarto notebook is an interactive, editable tutorial for estimating group-time average treatment effects and event-study aggregations with `cdid` (implementing Bellégo, Benatia and Dortet-Bernadet 2025 and extending Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021). Every estimation call uses the public `cdid` interface directly so you can copy, modify, and run individual chunks in your own workflow. See [Get started](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/get-started.md) and the [User Guide home](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/README.md) for companion documentation.

The 16 sections contain 33 R chunks: 29 run automatically and four are disabled (`eval: false`) for optional use. Run setup and the DGP first, then work downward.

- **Fresh session after reinstall:** If you reinstall `cdid`, `did`, or `DRDID`, restart R before rendering or running chunks interactively so that namespace bindings and compiled symbols are loaded cleanly.
- **Working directory & fail-fast execution:** You can run chunks from either the repository root or `notebooks/`. The setup chunk resolves `simulate_panel.R` via a relative path, prepends `validation/.lib` when present (else uses your normal R library), and `error: false` stops on the first unexpected error.

```{r}
#| label: setup
proj_root <- if (file.exists("notebooks/simulate_panel.R")) "." else if (file.exists("simulate_panel.R")) ".." else stop("Cannot locate simulate_panel.R.")
val_lib <- file.path(proj_root, "validation", ".lib")
if (dir.exists(val_lib)) .libPaths(c(normalizePath(val_lib, winslash = "/"), .libPaths()))

library(cdid); library(did); library(DRDID); library(knitr); library(ggplot2)

pkg_info <- data.frame(
  package  = c("R", "cdid", "did", "DRDID", "knitr", "ggplot2"),
  version  = c(as.character(getRversion()),
               vapply(c("cdid", "did", "DRDID", "knitr", "ggplot2"),
                      function(p) as.character(utils::packageVersion(p)), character(1))),
  directory_name = c(basename(R.home()), basename(find.package(c("cdid", "did", "DRDID", "knitr", "ggplot2")))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(pkg_info, caption = "Loaded versions and directory names (not full paths)")
source(file.path(proj_root, "notebooks", "simulate_panel.R"))
```

For local troubleshooting, run `find.package("cdid")` interactively to inspect its full installed path. The rendered table shows directory names only.

## 2. Editable DGP Configuration, Panel Draw, and Known Truth {#guide-2}

All examples in this core guide share a single synthetic study population controlled by the editable `cfg` chunk below. One call to `simulate_panel(cfg)` draws the **study-unit table** `units` (passed to `cdid` as `frame = units`) of size $N$ across $T$ calendar dates, constructs the latent complete outcomes, and applies observation masks to the **same underlying potential outcomes** without redrawing samples. The defaults use dates $1, \dots, 6$ and cohorts $3, 4, 5$, so each treated cohort has an untreated reference date $g - 1$. If you change the cohorts, update the matching `cohort_intercepts` and `treat_x_slope` vectors, keep them within the generated calendar, and retain a pretreatment reference date for the tutorial comparisons. Smaller samples or extreme probabilities can leave a cohort empty or cause a model/support refusal; the guide does not redraw such samples.

1. **Study population and cohorts (`units`):** Each study unit $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ is drawn i.i.d. from the superpopulation distribution defined by `cfg`, with binary covariate $X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_x)$, standard normal covariate $Z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, cluster label $c(i) \in \{1, \dots, C\}$, and treatment cohort $G_i \in \{0, 3, 4, 5\}$ with multinomial log-odds $\alpha_g + \beta_{g,x} X_i$ relative to never-treated controls $G_i = 0$.
2. **Untreated potential outcomes and within-unit changes:** $Y_{i,t}(0) = \alpha_i + (\delta + \theta_x X_i + \theta_z Z_i + u_{c(i)}) t + \varepsilon_{i,t}$, where $\alpha_i = \gamma_x X_i + \eta_i$ cancels in every within-unit change $Y_{i,t} - Y_{i,s}$, leaving $E[Y_{i,t}(0) - Y_{i,s}(0) \mid X_i, Z_i, G_i = 0] = (t - s)(\delta + \theta_x X_i + \theta_z Z_i)$ under `cluster_trend_sd = 0`.
3. **Treatment effects (`anticipation = 0`):** For $G_i = g > 0$ and $t \ge g$, $\tau_{i,t}(g) = \tau_0 + \tau_{\text{slope}}(t - g) + \tau_x X_i$.
4. **Observation masks on the same latent outcomes:**
   - `balanced_panel`: all $N \times T$ outcomes observed.
   - `missing_panel`: date $t$ is observed independently with probability $q_{i,t} = \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta_0 + \eta_t (t - 1) + \eta_x X_i + \eta_z Z_i + \eta_{\text{treat}}\mathbf{1}\{G_i > 0\})$, setting unobserved `y = NA_real_` while keeping all $N \times T$ rows in `data` and all $N$ study units in `units`. By default $\eta_z = 0$ (`obs_z_slope = 0`); if you set `obs_z_slope != 0`, the joint pair probability $q_{i,s} q_{i,t}$ is a product of two logistic functions of continuous $Z_i$ and is not itself a logistic regression linear in `x + z`.
   - `rotating_panel`: each study unit is observed only on one uniformly drawn consecutive two-date window $\{w_i, w_i + 1\}$ (`y = NA_real_` elsewhere).

```{r}
#| label: dgp-config
cfg <- default_dgp_config(
  n_units           = 2000L,                  # Study population size N in `units` (frame)
  n_periods         = 6L,                     # Stored calendar dates t = 1, ..., T
  seed              = 20261029L,              # Fixed RNG seed for reproducible synthetic draw
  cohorts           = c(3L, 4L, 5L),          # Positive treatment cohorts (0 = never treated)
  cohort_intercepts = c(-0.35, -0.45, -0.40), # Baseline log-odds vs G = 0 when x = 0
  treat_x_slope     = c(0.55, 0.35, -0.25),   # Log-odds shift per cohort when binary x = 1
  prob_x            = 0.50,                   # P(x = 1) for binary unit covariate x
  n_clusters        = 100L,                   # Number of clusters in `units`
  cluster_trend_sd  = 0.00,                   # 0.00 = IID baseline (set > 0 for cluster trend exercises)
  unit_sd           = 1.00,                   # SD of time-invariant unit fixed effect alpha_i
  unit_x_shift      = 0.40,                   # Shift in alpha_i when x = 1 (cancels in within-unit changes)
  time_trend        = 0.20,                   # Common per-period untreated trend
  trend_x           = 0.30,                   # Per-period untreated trend slope on binary x
  trend_z           = 0.15,                   # Per-period untreated trend slope on normal z
  effect_level      = 1.00,                   # Treatment effect intercept at onset e = t - g = 0
  effect_slope      = 0.25,                   # Treatment effect slope per event-time step e = t - g
  effect_x          = 0.50,                   # Treatment effect heterogeneity on binary x
  noise_sd          = 0.50,                   # SD of idiosyncratic normal shock eps_{i,t}
  obs_intercept     = 0.25,                   # Date-observation log-odds intercept at t = 1, x = 0
  obs_time_slope    = 0.08,                   # Per-period shift in date-observation log-odds
  obs_x_slope       = 0.55,                   # Shift in date-observation log-odds when x = 1
  obs_z_slope       = 0.00,                   # Shift in date-observation log-odds on normal z
  obs_treat_shift   = 0.00                    # Shift in date-observation log-odds for treated cohorts G > 0
)

sim <- simulate_panel(cfg)
units <- sim$units; balanced_panel <- sim$balanced_panel
missing_panel <- sim$missing_panel; rotating_panel <- sim$rotating_panel
```

### Superpopulation distribution vs realized study units and truth benchmarks {#truth-benchmarks}

The **superpopulation** is the probability distribution specified by `cfg`, from which a study could be drawn repeatedly. Its cohort probabilities and covariate means are analytical benchmarks. The **realized study units** are the finite set actually drawn into `units` (2000 by default), supplied to `cdid` as `frame = units`. Their counts and means vary across draws.

The helper calls the study-unit table a *roster*. Its API keeps the legacy fields `roster_latent_mean`, `roster_share`, `roster_g_share`, and `roster_x_mean`. For display, `study_truth` below copies the truth tables and renames `roster_latent_mean` to `study_unit_latent_mean` and `roster_share` to `study_unit_share`; `sim$truth` retains its original fields.

The first table compares the realized study units with the superpopulation across cohorts $g \in \{0, 3, 4, 5\}$:

| Displayed column in `cohort_tab` | Source in `units` / `sim$truth` | Meaning and why values differ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cohort` | `names(sim$truth$pop_prob_g)` | Cohort label $g \in \{0, 3, 4, 5\}$ (`0` = never-treated controls; `3, 4, 5` = treatment start dates). |
| `study_units` | `table(units$g)` | Realized integer count $N_g = \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{1}\{G_i = g\}$ of study units drawn into cohort $g$ (summing to $N = 2000$). |
| `study_unit_share` | $N_g / N$ (`sim$truth$roster_g_share` for $g > 0$) | Realized cohort share. It can differ from `pop_prob_g` because cohort counts fluctuate across draws. |
| `pop_prob_g` | `sim$truth$pop_prob_g` | Exact superpopulation probability $P(G = g) = (1 - p_x)P(G = g \mid X = 0) + p_x P(G = g \mid X = 1)$ (summing to $1$). |
| `pop_ex_given_g` | `sim$truth$pop_ex_given_g` | Exact superpopulation conditional mean $E[X \mid G = g] = P(X = 1 \mid G = g)$ computed by Bayes' rule. |
| `study_unit_x_mean` | $\bar{X}_g$ in `units` (`sim$truth$roster_x_mean` for $g > 0$) | Realized mean $\bar{X}_g = N_g^{-1}\sum_{i: G_i = g} X_i$. It can differ from `pop_ex_given_g` because the covariate composition fluctuates within cohorts. |

Correspondingly, `sim$truth` stores two distinct effect benchmarks and their aggregation weights:

| Field in `sim$truth` | Mathematical definition | Role in truth tables (`cells`, `dynamic`, `group`, `calendar`, `overall`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `population_att` | $\tau_0 + \tau_{\text{slope}}(t - g) + \tau_x E[X \mid G = g]$ | Superpopulation $\text{ATT}(g, t)$, using `pop_ex_given_g`; aggregated with population cohort weights. |
| `roster_latent_mean` (displayed as `study_unit_latent_mean`) | $\tau_0 + \tau_{\text{slope}}(t - g) + \tau_x \bar{X}_g$ | Latent mean treatment effect among the realized study units; aggregated with realized cohort weights. |
| `pop_cohort_share` | $P(G = g)$ for treated cohorts | Population cohort masses in `sim$truth$cells`, normalized over the cells/cohorts entering each weighted average. |
| `roster_share` (displayed as `study_unit_share`) | $N_g / N$ for treated cohorts | Realized cohort masses in `sim$truth$cells`, normalized in the corresponding weighted averages. |

```{r}
#| label: inspect-draw-and-truth
study_truth <- lapply(sim$truth[c("cells", "dynamic", "group", "calendar", "overall")], function(tab) {
  names(tab)[names(tab) == "roster_latent_mean"] <- "study_unit_latent_mean"
  names(tab)[names(tab) == "roster_share"] <- "study_unit_share"
  tab
})
cohort_levels <- names(sim$truth$pop_prob_g)
cohort_counts <- as.integer(table(factor(units$g, levels = cohort_levels)))
cohort_tab <- data.frame(
  cohort            = cohort_levels,
  study_units       = cohort_counts,
  study_unit_share  = round(cohort_counts / nrow(units), 4),
  pop_prob_g        = round(unname(sim$truth$pop_prob_g), 4),
  pop_ex_given_g    = round(unname(sim$truth$pop_ex_given_g), 4),
  study_unit_x_mean = round(as.numeric(tapply(units$x, factor(units$g, levels = cohort_levels), mean)), 4)
)
knitr::kable(cohort_tab, caption = "Realized study units vs superpopulation cohort probabilities")
list(
  missing_panel_dates_per_unit  = table(observed_dates = tapply(!is.na(missing_panel$y), missing_panel$id, sum)),
  rotating_panel_dates_per_unit = table(observed_dates = tapply(!is.na(rotating_panel$y), rotating_panel$id, sum))
)
knitr::kable(study_truth$cells, digits = 4, caption = "Analytic superpopulation ATT vs realized study-unit latent mean effect by (g, t)")
knitr::kable(study_truth$overall, digits = 4, caption = "Overall aggregation truth benchmarks across all four aggte types")
```

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- Compare `population_att` and `study_unit_latent_mean`. Cell benchmarks can differ when `effect_x != 0` because $\bar{X}_g$ fluctuates around $E[X \mid G = g]$; aggregate benchmarks can also differ because their cohort weights differ. Both average noiseless treatment effects. Estimates from noisy outcomes need not equal either benchmark in one draw.
- Units observed at $0$ or $1$ dates supply no outcome differences, yet remain in `units` so cohort shares, observation models fitted on all study units ([Section 5](#selection-universe-and-pooling)), and $N$-row influence functions cover the study population. See [Prepare your panel and unit table](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/prepare-data.md).
- **Try changing:** Set `effect_x = 0` in `cfg` to make the cell effects homogeneous across $X_i$. The two cell benchmarks then coincide; their aggregates can still differ when realized cohort composition shifts the weights on different event times. Reduce `n_units` to explore finite-sample variation. If you set `cluster_trend_sd > 0`, pass `clustervars = "cluster"` in your estimation calls ([Section 10](#guide-10)) for inference that accounts for the shared cluster trend; supplying cluster labels in `units` alone does not request clustered inference.

## 3. Explore Missingness and Pair Support Before Estimation {#guide-3}

Before fitting any model on an incomplete or rotating panel, inspect the study-unit table `units`, count observed dates per study unit (including zero-outcome and single-outcome units), and tabulate how many study units are observed at both endpoints of key date pairs. A study unit with two observed dates supplies only that specific pair, not every pair in the calendar. These raw counts require only `units` and the panel dataset (no fitted object) and reveal sample support before estimation; fitted target availability is inspected later in [Section 7](#fitted-support) once the missing-panel and rotating-panel fits exist. Counts diagnose support; they do not verify the mean-change or parallel-trends assumptions. See [Investigate missingness and data structure](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/investigate-missingness.md) and [Diagnose errors and unavailable results](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/troubleshooting.md).

```{r}
#| label: missingness-counts
panel_to_explore <- missing_panel  # Set to missing_panel or rotating_panel to inspect raw counts before fitting.
obs_data <- transform(panel_to_explore, observed = as.integer(!is.na(y)))
unit_counts <- merge(units[, c("id", "g")],
  aggregate(observed ~ id, data = obs_data, FUN = sum), by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
unit_counts$observed[is.na(unit_counts$observed)] <- 0L
study_unit_counts <- aggregate(id ~ g, data = units, FUN = length)
names(study_unit_counts)[2] <- "study_units"
date_counts <- merge(aggregate(observed ~ g + time, data = obs_data, FUN = sum),
                     study_unit_counts, by = "g")
date_counts$observed_share <- date_counts$observed / date_counts$study_units
knitr::kable(date_counts, digits = 3, caption = "Observed outcomes by cohort and date over study-population denominators (study_units)")
table(observed_dates = unit_counts$observed)
data.frame(study_units = nrow(units), stored_rows = nrow(panel_to_explore),
           zero_dates = sum(unit_counts$observed == 0), one_date = sum(unit_counts$observed == 1),
           repeat_observers = sum(unit_counts$observed >= 2))
```

Choose a few pairs to investigate rather than constructing a dense unit-by-date matrix or enumerating every possible pair. Here the defaults select the first adjacent pair, the last adjacent pair, and the first-to-last pair; duplicate choices are removed on a short calendar. Edit `pairs_to_check` to examine the dates relevant to your question.

```{r}
#| label: missingness-pair-support
explore_dates <- sort(unique(panel_to_explore$time))
last_date <- length(explore_dates)
pairs_to_check <- unique(data.frame(
  s = c(explore_dates[1], explore_dates[last_date - 1L], explore_dates[1]),
  t = c(explore_dates[2], explore_dates[last_date], explore_dates[last_date])))
pair_counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(pairs_to_check)), function(j) {
  s <- pairs_to_check$s[j]; t <- pairs_to_check$t[j]
  ids_s <- obs_data$id[obs_data$time == s & obs_data$observed == 1L]
  ids_t <- obs_data$id[obs_data$time == t & obs_data$observed == 1L]
  joint_ids <- intersect(ids_s, ids_t)
  data.frame(cohort = study_unit_counts$g, s = s, t = t,
    study_units = study_unit_counts$study_units,
    observed_pairs = vapply(study_unit_counts$g, function(k)
      sum(units$id[units$g == k] %in% joint_ids), numeric(1)))
}))
pair_counts$observed_share <- pair_counts$observed_pairs / pair_counts$study_units
knitr::kable(pair_counts, digits = 3, caption = "Selected-pair counts, including zeros, over study-population denominators (study_units)")
```

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- Inspect `zero_dates`, `one_date`, and `repeat_observers` alongside the cohort-level `study_units` denominator in `date_counts` and `pair_counts`. Every study unit in `units` remains part of the study population denominator `study_units`, even when it has `0` or `1` observed outcomes and therefore contributes `0` observed outcome pairs.
- **Try changing:** Switch `panel_to_explore` to `rotating_panel` and rerun both chunks. Each study unit has `observed_dates == 2`; only adjacent pairs can have positive `observed_pairs`, and the long-span pair $(1,6)$ has zero in every cohort. After estimating `fit_miss_date` ([Section 5](#guide-5)) and `fit_rot` ([Section 7](#guide-7)), inspect [fitted target availability](#fitted-support) to compare these counts with cell-level support reasons.

## 4. Balanced Panel Baseline: Group-Time Estimation and Aggregations {#guide-4}

We begin estimation with a direct balanced-panel fit on `balanced_panel` using `cdid::att_gt()`. Because both $X_i$ and $Z_i$ shift untreated outcome trends ($\theta_x = 0.30$, $\theta_z = 0.15$) and $X_i$ also shifts cohort assignment, we pass `xformla = ~ x + z` with doubly robust treatment adjustment (`est_method = "dr"`), never-treated controls (`control_group = "nevertreated"`), and parallel trends from each cohort's reference period (`pt_assumption = "post"`). Analytical standard errors (`bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE`) give fast interactive feedback; `cdid::tidy()`, `cdid::glance()`, and `cdid::ggdid()` inspect the cell-level results. See [Get started](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/get-started.md) and the [Results reference](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md).

```{r}
#| label: balanced-att-gt
fit_bal <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = balanced_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
summary(fit_bal)
```

```{r}
#| label: balanced-tidy-glance-plot
bal_cells <- merge(
  cdid::tidy(fit_bal)[, c("target.id", "group", "time", "role", "estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "available")],
  study_truth$cells[, c("target.id", "population_att", "study_unit_latent_mean")],
  by = "target.id", all.x = TRUE
)
knitr::kable(bal_cells, digits = 4, caption = "Balanced-panel group-time estimates and truth benchmarks")
knitr::kable(cdid::glance(fit_bal), digits = 4, caption = "Single-row glance summary of fit_bal")
cdid::ggdid(fit_bal)
```

### Four aggregations: simple, group, dynamic, and calendar

`cdid::aggte()` aggregates the stored group-time estimates without refitting nuisance models, propagating cohort-share uncertainty from the study-unit table `units` through the stored $N$-row influence functions ([Aggregated results](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#aggregated-results)).

```{r}
#| label: balanced-aggte-simple-group
agg_bal_simple <- cdid::aggte(fit_bal, type = "simple")
agg_bal_group  <- cdid::aggte(fit_bal, type = "group")
summary(agg_bal_simple); summary(agg_bal_group)
cdid::ggdid(agg_bal_group)
```

```{r}
#| label: balanced-aggte-dynamic-calendar
agg_bal_dynamic  <- cdid::aggte(fit_bal, type = "dynamic")
agg_bal_calendar <- cdid::aggte(fit_bal, type = "calendar")
summary(agg_bal_dynamic)
knitr::kable(
  merge(cdid::tidy(agg_bal_dynamic)[, c("event.time", "estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "available")],
        study_truth$dynamic, by.x = "event.time", by.y = "event_time", all.x = TRUE),
  digits = 4, caption = "Dynamic event-study estimates vs superpopulation and realized study-unit benchmarks"
)
cdid::ggdid(agg_bal_dynamic); cdid::ggdid(agg_bal_calendar)
```

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- With multiple treated cohorts ($G \in \{3, 4, 5\}$), `"simple"` weights every posttreatment cell by its cohort share, `"group"` averages within each cohort first and then weights cohorts by their shares, `"dynamic"` averages equally across event times $e \ge 0$, and `"calendar"` averages equally across calendar periods $t \ge 3$.
- **Try changing:** Set `bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE, biters = 500` in `fit_bal` (after `set.seed(1)`) for simultaneous multiplier bootstrap bands ([Section 10](#guide-10)).

## 5. Incomplete Panels, Study Units, and Observation Models (`conditional_mtar`) {#guide-5}

In `missing_panel`, unobserved outcomes are coded as `y = NA_real_` while all $N \times T = 12000$ rows remain in `data` and all $N = 2000$ study units remain in `frame = units`. See [Handling missing outcomes](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md) and [Choose an observation model](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/observation-models.md).

- **Why `data` and `frame` play distinct roles:** A study unit must be observed at both endpoints of a pair $(s, t)$ to contribute $\Delta Y_{i,s,t} = Y_{i,t} - Y_{i,s}$. Units observed at zero or one date supply no differences, but remain in `frame = units` for cohort shares, observation models fitted on all study units, and $N$-row influence functions.
- **Why `selection = "none"` lacks its required mean restriction here:** For each used pair, `selection = "none"` requires the observed pair sample to be representative of its cohort's **mean outcome change** without an observation adjustment. This is a population mean condition, not a claim that each unit has the cohort mean or that realized sample means are equal. In our default DGP, units with $X_i = 1$ are observed more often (`obs_x_slope = 0.55`) and have a larger untreated trend ($\theta_x = 0.30$) and larger treatment effect ($\tau_x = 0.50$). Even though `est_method = "dr"` adjusts for covariate differences **between** treated and control cohorts, it does not by itself reconstruct missing treated changes for the study population. Pair-specific observation can select different compositions, so the resulting GMM moments need not describe one common selected subpopulation and can bias the full-population ATT.

### First-use definitions: `selection_universe = "F"` and `selection_pooling = "separate"` {#selection-universe-and-pooling}

The corrected calls use `selection = "conditional_mtar"` and `selection_est_method = "ipw"`, with two arguments to understand first:

**`selection_universe = "F"` fits observation models on all $N$ rows of `frame = units`**, including units observed once or never. These models use binary responses: observed at the required date or pair is a success; otherwise it is a failure. They do not form nonexistent outcome differences. `"F"` means the full study-unit table, not complete outcome cases. Every observed change still needs both endpoints, whatever the fitting set, and `frame` defines the target study population.

The restricted sets `"B"` ($\ge 1$ observed outcome) and `"A"` ($\ge 2$) are available only for pair logits under observation weighting, with explicit representativeness or transport justification. Choose these through arguments; keep `units` and `data` intact. See [Section 7](#guide-7) and [Sampling information for the observation model](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/sampling-information.md).

**`selection_pooling = "separate"` shares no slopes across cells** and gives each cell a free intercept when `selection_xformla` includes one:

- `selection_model = "pair_logit"` fits a logit per needed cohort-and-pair cell $(k,s,t)$ for $R_{i,s}R_{i,t}=1$. With binary $X_i$ and `obs_z_slope = 0`, `~ x` is saturated in each cell. With observation depending on continuous $Z_i$, a pair logit on `~ x + z` generally cannot represent the product of two date logits.
- `selection_model = "independent_period_logit"` fits a logit per needed cohort-and-date cell $(k,t)$ for $R_{i,t}=1$, then multiplies the endpoint probabilities. This requires conditional independence of the two dates given cohort and covariates ([Section 7](#date-independence-and-rotation)).

For shared slope options, see [Section 7](#guide-7) and [Pooling: how much the models share](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#pooling-how-much-the-models-share).

```{r}
#| label: missing-none-vs-pair
fit_miss_none <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_miss_pair <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "pair_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: missing-date-logit-and-compare
fit_miss_date <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
agg_miss_list <- list(none_invalid = cdid::aggte(fit_miss_none, type = "simple"),
                      pair_logit   = cdid::aggte(fit_miss_pair, type = "simple"),
                      date_logit   = cdid::aggte(fit_miss_date, type = "simple"))
miss_comp <- data.frame(
  specification      = names(agg_miss_list),
  simple_att         = vapply(agg_miss_list, function(a) a$overall.att, numeric(1)),
  std_error          = vapply(agg_miss_list, function(a) a$overall.se, numeric(1)),
  population_att         = study_truth$overall$population_att[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  study_unit_latent_mean = study_truth$overall$study_unit_latent_mean[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  row.names          = NULL
)
knitr::kable(miss_comp, digits = 6, caption = "Simple ATT under missingness (6-decimal precision): unadjusted selection = 'none' vs pair and date observation models")
```

### Interpreting the 6-decimal standard errors in `miss_comp` {#missingness-se-comparison}

At four decimals, all three `std_error` values round to `0.0292`. At six decimals, the default draw gives `0.029188` (none), `0.029185` (pair), and `0.029169` (date). A check of their stored influence functions reconstructed each SE as $\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(\mathrm{IF}^2)/N}$ with $N=2000$, and found different unit-level IFs across fits. This checks the displayed SEs; it does not verify nuisance propagation or inference validity.

As documented in [Analytical standard errors and clustering](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#analytical-standard-errors-and-clustering), analytical SEs use the complete original-unit influence function, including estimated $q$, $j$, $p$, and $m$ **when active**, plus the response rates and cohort shares used by the method. No $q$ is fitted under `selection = "none"` or pure imputation; $p$ is active only for treatment IPW/DR, $m$ for OR/DR, and $j$ for imputation/augmentation. The variance includes covariance between the direct and nuisance-estimation terms, so estimating weights does not necessarily increase variance. Valid population inference still requires the chosen method's identification, model, overlap, and regularity conditions.

Similar precision is plausible here: the fits share outcomes and noise, aim at the same population target, and the corrected routes use simple correct logits with moderate observation probabilities. Closeness does not imply that observation-model estimation was ignored. The unadjusted route has unsupported population mean-change restrictions and can be biased; neither its reported SE nor this comparison justifies a population ATT or confidence-interval claim. See [How to compare precision](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/precision.md).

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- Compare `miss_comp` with `population_att` and the realized study-unit benchmark `study_unit_latent_mean`. The pair and date routes adjust for the default observation law; `none_invalid` lacks the required mean restriction. One draw does not measure bias.
- **Try changing:** Set `obs_x_slope = 0` in `cfg` and rerun [Section 2](#guide-2) and [Section 5](#guide-5). With the remaining defaults, observation is independent of outcome changes within each cohort, restoring the mean restriction for `selection = "none"`. Setting `effect_x = 0` alone removes effect heterogeneity but need not make untreated changes representative when observation still depends on $X_i$. Alternatively, lower `obs_intercept` / increase `obs_x_slope` to explore weight dispersion and compare the resulting SEs.

## 6. Treatment Adjustment (`ipw`, `reg`, `dr`) with Distinct `selection_xformla` {#guide-6}

`cdid` separates **treatment adjustment** (`est_method` and `xformla`; see [Treatment adjustment](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/treatment.md)) from **missing-outcome adjustment** (`selection`, `selection_est_method`, and `selection_xformla`; see [Two covariate formulas](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#two-covariate-formulas)):

- **`xformla = ~ x + z`** supplies the predictors for the treatment propensity logits $p$ (`est_method = "ipw"` or `"dr"`) and for the pooled control outcome-change regression $m$ (`est_method = "reg"` or `"dr"`). In our default DGP with `control_group = "nevertreated"`, both models are correctly specified: each cohort's log-odds against $G_i = 0$ are linear in $(X_i, Z_i)$, and the control mean change $(t - s)(\delta + \theta_x X_i + \theta_z Z_i)$ matches `cdid`'s duration-scaled regression $m_b(X_i, Z_i) = \alpha(b) + L(e)(X_i \beta_x + Z_i \beta_z)$ with $L(e) = t - s$.
- **`selection_xformla = ~ x`** supplies a distinct predictor list used only for the observation model $q$. Leaving `selection_xformla = NULL` would inherit `xformla = ~ x + z`; setting `selection_xformla = ~ x` explicitly restricts the observation logits to the binary covariate $X_i$ that drives observation in the DGP.

```{r}
#| label: treat-ipw-and-reg
fit_treat_ipw <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "ipw",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)

fit_treat_reg <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "reg",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: treat-dr-and-table
fit_treat_dr <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)

treat_agg <- list(ipw = cdid::aggte(fit_treat_ipw, type = "simple"),
                  reg = cdid::aggte(fit_treat_reg, type = "simple"),
                  dr  = cdid::aggte(fit_treat_dr, type = "simple"))
treat_table <- data.frame(
  est_method         = names(treat_agg),
  estimator_label    = c(fit_treat_ipw$chained$estimator, fit_treat_reg$chained$estimator, fit_treat_dr$chained$estimator),
  simple_att         = vapply(treat_agg, function(a) a$overall.att, numeric(1)),
  std_error          = vapply(treat_agg, function(a) a$overall.se, numeric(1)),
  population_att         = study_truth$overall$population_att[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  study_unit_latent_mean = study_truth$overall$study_unit_latent_mean[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  row.names          = NULL
)
knitr::kable(treat_table, digits = 6, caption = "Treatment adjustment comparison (ipw, reg, dr; 6-decimal precision) on missing_panel with selection_xformla = ~ x")
```

### Reading the treatment-adjustment standard errors {#treatment-se-comparison}

Treatment IPW relies on $p$, OR (`"reg"`) on $m$, and DR on either correct model under the remaining assumptions ([Choose IPW, OR or DR](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/treatment-choice.md)). These are distinct functionals: correct models do not imply equal finite-sample estimates, influence functions, or SEs. The default SEs are `0.029236` (IPW), `0.028984` (OR), and `0.029169` (DR).

The nearby values occur in a mild design with binary treatment predictors, correct $p$ and $m$, modest continuous trend variation, and shared outcomes and date-logit observation weights. They give no general efficiency ranking or coverage evidence; the [SE qualifications in Section 5](#missingness-se-comparison) apply here too.

**Try changing:** Increase `trend_z` in `cfg`, redraw once, and refit to explore the role of outcome regression when untreated changes vary more with $Z_i$. Alternatively, keep this draw and omit `z` from `xformla`, or increase `treat_x_slope` before redrawing to explore weaker overlap. Inspect the resulting SEs without assuming an ordering. For separate $p$/$m$ misspecification exercises, see [Section 12](#guide-12).

## 7. Selection Slope Pooling, Date Independence, Rotating Panels, and Support Diagnostics {#guide-7}

As introduced in [Section 5](#selection-universe-and-pooling), `selection_pooling` controls whether observation logits estimate separate covariate slopes per cell (`"separate"`), share one slope vector per cohort across its dates or pairs (`"within_cohort"`), or share a single slope vector across all cohorts and dates/pairs (`"across_cohorts"`). Every cell retains its own free intercept whenever `selection_xformla` includes an intercept ([Pooling: how much the models share](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#pooling-how-much-the-models-share)). In our default DGP, the date-observation log-odds are $\eta_0 + \eta_t (t - 1) + \eta_x X_i$ with $\eta_x = 0.55$ and $\eta_{\text{treat}} = 0$, so all three `selection_pooling` choices are correctly specified for `selection_model = "independent_period_logit"`. (Under `selection_model = "pair_logit"`, the log-odds of $q_{i,s} q_{i,t}$ do not have a constant slope across pairs with different baseline intercepts, so pooling pair-logit slopes across pairs would be misspecified; see [How much the logits share](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/observation-models.md#how-much-the-logits-share).)

```{r}
#| label: selection-pooling-within-across
fit_pool_within <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "within_cohort", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_pool_across <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "across_cohorts", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)

pool_agg <- list(separate = treat_agg$dr,
                 within_cohort = cdid::aggte(fit_pool_within, type = "simple"),
                 across_cohorts = cdid::aggte(fit_pool_across, type = "simple"))
pool_table <- data.frame(
  selection_pooling = names(pool_agg),
  n_selection_fits  = c(fit_treat_dr$chained$selection$models$n_selection_fits,
                        fit_pool_within$chained$selection$models$n_selection_fits,
                        fit_pool_across$chained$selection$models$n_selection_fits),
  simple_att        = vapply(pool_agg, function(a) a$overall.att, numeric(1)),
  std_error         = vapply(pool_agg, function(a) a$overall.se, numeric(1)),
  row.names         = NULL
)
knitr::kable(pool_table, digits = 6, caption = "Date-logit slope pooling under common population slopes on F (6-decimal precision)")
```

The default fitting universe `"F"` uses all study units in `frame = units`. For observation weighting with `selection_model = "pair_logit"` only, `selection_universe = "B"` fits pair logits on study units with at least one observed outcome and `"A"` on study units with at least two observed outcomes. Those restricted fitting sets still target the full study population `"F"` and require an explicit `selection_justification` plus the documented representativeness or known normalized density-ratio (`selection_rho`) transport conditions; never trim `units` or `data` to form a subset manually. See [Advanced: fitting the observation model on part of the unit table](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#advanced-fitting-the-observation-model-on-part-of-the-unit-table) and [Sampling information for the observation model](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/sampling-information.md).

### Study-unit retention and date independence are separate requirements {#date-independence-and-rotation}

Keeping all study units in `"F"` preserves the population denominator and lets date models describe that population. Multiplying their probabilities additionally requires conditional independence for every used pair in the original population:

$$P(R_{i,s}=1,R_{i,t}=1\mid X_i,G_i)
=P(R_{i,s}=1\mid X_i,G_i)P(R_{i,t}=1\mid X_i,G_i).$$

The full table cannot create this independence. Conversely, conditioning on at least two observed dates (`"A"`) can make date indicators dependent even when they were independent in `"F"`. This is why date logits require `selection_universe = "F"`; retaining the table and justifying the probability product are separate tasks.

In `rotating_panel`, each unit has exactly two consecutive observed dates and no unit is a singleton. Non-adjacent dates have positive marginal observation probabilities but zero joint probability, so their product is wrong. Even adjacent endpoints need not be independent: knowing one date is observed restricts the possible window assignments. No singleton is needed for this violation.

For fixed planned-window rotation, date products are generally inappropriate. Our uniformly assigned windows justify `selection = "none"` because window assignment is independent of cohort mean changes. When supported-pair observation instead depends on covariates, use a valid observed-pair model, or justified imputation/augmentation with its own support and model conditions. The actual design law matters; the label “rotating” alone does not decide validity.

Unsupported distant pairs do not prevent valid adjacent chaining. Check positivity, cohort/control support, and the mean-change and trend conditions on the comparisons actually used. Supported adjacent links can then recover longer-horizon effects through GMM. An all-zero unsupported pair cannot fit a logit with a free intercept, and imputation cannot create positivity or training support for that pair. See [Which changes are available](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#which-changes-are-available).

```{r}
#| label: rotating-panel-chained-fit
fit_rot <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = rotating_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
agg_rot_dyn <- cdid::aggte(fit_rot, type = "dynamic")
knitr::kable(
  merge(cdid::tidy(agg_rot_dyn)[, c("event.time", "estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "available")],
        study_truth$dynamic, by.x = "event.time", by.y = "event_time", all.x = TRUE),
  digits = 4, caption = "Chained dynamic event-study estimates on rotating_panel (consecutive two-date windows)"
)
```

### Inspect fitted target availability and support diagnostics {#fitted-support}

After fitting `fit_miss_date` ([Section 5](#guide-5)) or `fit_rot` (above), use `cdid::tidy(fit_to_explore)` to complement the raw counts in [Section 3](#guide-3). It returns one row per requested cohort-date target; `knitr::kable()` only formats the table.

| Column | How to read it |
| --- | --- |
| `target.id` | Identifier such as `"ATT(g=3,t=6)"`. |
| `group`, `time` | Cohort $g$ and calendar date $t$. |
| `role` | `"pre"` for pre-reference reports, `"post"` for posttreatment effects, or `"reference"` for exact-zero universal reference cells. |
| `available` | Whether the estimator can recover/report the target from retained comparisons under the selected settings. |
| `support.status` | Short code, such as `estimable` or `supported_direct_pretrend`; read it together with `available`. |
| `support.reason` | Explanation of the supporting comparison/chain, or why the target is unavailable. A reason can also be present when `available = TRUE`. |

`available = TRUE` does not verify scientific assumptions or population identification. A missing direct long-span comparison need not make the target unavailable: a valid chain can supply it. Switch to `fit_rot` below to inspect this distinction.

Unavailable cells have `NA` estimates, SEs, and influence-function columns; unavailable never means zero. An aggregate requiring such cells is also `NA` with a reason, unless `na.rm = TRUE` explicitly requests a different, restricted target. Inspect reasons rather than silently discarding cells. See [Tables from tidy and glance](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#tables-from-tidy-and-glance), [Unavailable effects](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#unavailable-effects), and [An effect is unavailable](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/troubleshooting.md#an-effect-is-unavailable).

```{r}
#| label: fitted-support-diagnostics
fit_to_explore <- fit_miss_date  # Set to fit_miss_date (Section 5), fit_miss_pair (Section 5), or fit_rot (above).
knitr::kable(
  cdid::tidy(fit_to_explore)[, c("target.id", "group", "time", "role", "available", "support.status", "support.reason")],
  caption = "Target-level availability and support diagnostics from cdid::tidy(fit_to_explore)"
)
list(study_unit_rows      = nrow(fit_to_explore$chained$frame),
     influence_dimensions = dim(fit_to_explore$inffunc))
```

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- Confirm that `study_unit_rows` (`nrow(fit_to_explore$chained$frame)`) and the row dimension of `fit_to_explore$inffunc` both equal $N = 2000$, the full study-unit table `units`.
- **Try changing:** Switch `fit_to_explore` to `fit_rot` (and pair it with `panel_to_explore <- rotating_panel` in [Section 3](#guide-3)) to compare the raw pair support counts with the fitted target availability table.

## 8. Observation Weighting vs Change Imputation and Augmented Double-DR {#guide-8}

To correct for covariate-dependent missingness on `selection_universe = "F"`, `selection = "conditional_mtar"` supports three `selection_est_method` routes ([How to adjust](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#how-to-adjust), [Impute actual changes for missing outcomes](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/change-imputation.md), and [Compare model robustness across treatment and missing outcome adjustments](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/robustness.md)):

1. **Observation weighting (`"ipw"`):** Reweights observed pair changes by the inverse observation probability $q_c(X)$.
2. **Pure actual-change imputation (`"imputation"`):** Fits a weighted least-squares regression $j_{k,e}(X, Z) = \alpha(k, e) + L(e)(X \beta_{x,r} + Z \beta_{z,r})$ to study units of cohort $k$ observed at both endpoints of pair $e = (s, t)$, then averages predictions across **all** study units of cohort $k$ in `frame = units` (leaving `y = NA` untouched in `data`). No observation model $q$ is fitted (`selection_model`, `selection_pooling`, and `selection_xformla` are omitted).
3. **Augmented / double-DR (`"dr"`):** Combines actual-change predictions $j_c(X, Z)$ with inverse-probability weighted residuals $S_{i,e}\{\Delta Y_{i,e} - j_c(X, Z)\}/\max(q_c(X_i), 10^{-6})$. Under valid conditional mean restrictions, support, and regularity conditions, its sufficient model condition is ($p$ or $m$ correct) and, for every used cell, ($q_c$ or $j_c$ correct). Pooled models must be correct across the cells sharing coefficients. The package floors inverse observation denominators at $10^{-6}$ and caps treatment propensities at $1 - 10^{-6}$; the usual original-target robustness statements require these safeguards to be inactive in the population or additional target-preserving conditions ([Probability safeguards](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#probability-safeguards)).

- **Counterfactual regression $m$ (`est_method = "reg"` or `"dr"`) vs actual-change regression $j$ (`selection_est_method = "imputation"` or `"dr"`):** $m$ models **untreated** changes among controls across all comparison blocks with one shared duration-scaled slope vector on $L(e)(X_i, Z_i)$, whereas $j$ models **actual** changes within each cohort $k$ and pair $e = (s, t)$, including treatment effects for treated cohorts. Because $X_i$ shifts the treatment effect by $\tau_x = 0.50$ at onset, any pair $e = (s, t)$ for cohort $g$ that crosses treatment onset ($s < g \le t$) has actual-change slope $\theta_x L(e) + \tau_x$ on $X_i$ (duration-scaled coefficient $\theta_x + \tau_x / L(e)$), whereas pairs entirely before or after $g$ have duration-scaled coefficient $\theta_x$. Thus `imputation_pooling = "separate"` is required here; pooling $j$ slopes via `"within_cohort"` or `"across_cohorts"` is misspecified whenever $\tau_x \neq 0$.

```{r}
#| label: imputation-and-augmented-dr
fit_sel_imp <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "imputation",
  selection_universe = "F", imputation_pooling = "separate",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_sel_aug <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "dr",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate",
  selection_universe = "F", imputation_pooling = "separate",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)

sel_routes <- list(obs_weighting = treat_agg$dr,
                   imputation    = cdid::aggte(fit_sel_imp, type = "simple"),
                   augmented_dr  = cdid::aggte(fit_sel_aug, type = "simple"))
sel_route_tab <- data.frame(
  selection_est_method = c("ipw", "imputation", "dr"),
  estimator_label      = c(fit_treat_dr$chained$estimator, fit_sel_imp$chained$estimator, fit_sel_aug$chained$estimator),
  simple_att           = vapply(sel_routes, function(a) a$overall.att, numeric(1)),
  std_error            = vapply(sel_routes, function(a) a$overall.se, numeric(1)),
  population_att         = study_truth$overall$population_att[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  study_unit_latent_mean = study_truth$overall$study_unit_latent_mean[study_truth$overall$type == "simple"],
  row.names            = NULL
)
knitr::kable(sel_route_tab, digits = 6, caption = "Observation weighting vs pure change imputation vs augmented double-DR (6-decimal precision)")
```

### Reading the observation-adjustment standard errors {#imputation-se-comparison}

In the observation layer, weighting uses $q$, imputation uses $j$, and augmentation uses both; all three calls also use treatment DR ($p$/$m$). Their default SEs are `0.029169`, `0.029055`, and `0.029079`, respectively. The stored IFs differ across routes. Correct models do not imply finite-sample equality, and augmentation is one reconstructed-change estimator, not an average of the other two.

Inspect `fit_sel_imp$chained$selection` and `fit_sel_aug$chained$selection` for the active-model records.

Shared outcomes, moderate observation probabilities driven by binary $X_i$, and correct models make nearby precision plausible in this mild design. This gives no general efficiency ranking or coverage evidence; see the [SE qualifications in Section 5](#missingness-se-comparison).

**Try changing:** Lower `obs_intercept` or increase `obs_x_slope` in `cfg`, redraw once, and refit to explore how observation rates and weight dispersion affect the three SEs. Alternatively, set `obs_z_slope = 0.50` and compare the current observation formula with `selection_xformla = ~ x + z`: omitting `z` misspecifies $q$ while separate-cell $j$ remains representable. Setting `effect_x = 0` instead makes the shared imputation slopes representable too. Keep support/model refusals visible.

## 9. Comparison Groups, Preperiod Reporting vs `PT-all`, and `did` Delegation {#guide-9}

- **`control_group = "notyettreated"`:** Allows later-treated cohorts that remain untreated at the comparison's control horizon, alongside $G = 0$ (with zero anticipation). The horizon is at least $\max(s, t)$; the chained catalog can reuse the same pair with a later horizon and a smaller eligible control pool, then combine those moments by GMM. In this DGP, cohort assignment depends only on **binary** $X_i$, so an intercept and `x` saturate each population risk-set treatment logit; the coefficient on `z` is zero. Mixing cohorts therefore does not itself misspecify that logit here. With continuous treatment predictors, a mixture can produce nonlinear risk-set log-odds. The shared untreated change regression $m$ remains correctly specified across the default control pools.
- **`base_period = "universal"` vs `pt_assumption = "all"` (`pt_start = 1`):** `base_period` is purely a **reporting choice** for unrestricted preperiod cells (`role == "pre"`): `"varying"` reports consecutive preperiod steps, whereas `"universal"` anchors every reported preperiod cell to each cohort's reference date $g - 1$ (with an exact zero reference row at $t = g - 1$). By contrast, `pt_assumption = "all"` with an explicit common calendar start date `pt_start = 1` adds **overidentifying GMM restrictions** setting untreated pre-reference trend differentials from date `pt_start = 1` up to each cohort's reference date to zero ([Parallel trends](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/parallel-trends.md)). Because conditional parallel trends hold across all dates $1, \dots, 6$ in our default DGP, both `PT-post` and `PT-all` (`pt_start = 1`) impose true population restrictions.

```{r}
#| label: nyt-universal-and-pt-all
fit_nyt_univ <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "notyettreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "universal", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_pt_all <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate", selection_universe = "F",
  pt_assumption = "all", pt_start = 1, base_period = "varying", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)

pt_comp <- data.frame(
  specification = c("NT + PT-post + varying", "NYT + PT-post + universal", "NT + PT-all (pt_start=1) + varying"),
  simple_att    = c(treat_agg$dr$overall.att,
                    cdid::aggte(fit_nyt_univ, type = "simple")$overall.att,
                    cdid::aggte(fit_pt_all, type = "simple")$overall.att),
  std_error     = c(treat_agg$dr$overall.se,
                    cdid::aggte(fit_nyt_univ, type = "simple")$overall.se,
                    cdid::aggte(fit_pt_all, type = "simple")$overall.se)
)
knitr::kable(pt_comp, digits = 6, caption = "Comparison across control_group, base_period, and PT-all (pt_start = 1; 6-decimal precision)")
```

### Ordinary `did` delegation (`mode = "ordinary"`) and when balanced fits agree or differ {#ordinary-did-delegation}

Setting `mode = "ordinary"` delegates directly to `did::att_gt()` ([Moving from did](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/from-did.md)). On `balanced_panel`, whether `mode = "chained"` and `mode = "ordinary"` produce identical estimates depends on the actual moment system and nuisance specifications fitted:

- **Exact algebraic reduction:** With a balanced panel, `control_group = "nevertreated"`, no covariates (`xformla = NULL`, `est_method = "ipw"`), equal unit weights, `selection = "none"`, `pt_assumption = "post"`, and matched anticipation and base-period settings, chained comparisons telescope algebraically to the long two-period differences computed by `did`, so point estimates are expected to agree up to floating-point rounding. This is a computational comparison. In our main DGP, omitting $X_i$ leaves cohort-related untreated trends unadjusted, so agreement of these two unadjusted fits does not establish identification of the ATT.
- **Why covariate-adjusted, NYT, or `PT-all` specifications can differ:** With covariates (`xformla = ~ x + z` under `"reg"` or `"dr"`), `cdid` fits one pooled control regression $m$ with duration-scaled slopes $L(e)(X_i, Z_i)'\beta$ and combines links via GMM, whereas `did` ordinarily fits separate pair-specific regressions. Different coefficient restrictions or fitting procedures can change finite-sample estimates; method labels alone do not imply a difference, and nuisance corrections can cancel. Likewise, `control_group = "notyettreated"` in chained GMM retains additional fixed-horizon control-pool comparisons, and `pt_assumption = "all"` adds pre-reference zero-differential GMM moments. No uniform precision ranking follows from these differences.

```{r}
#| label: ordinary-did-comparison
fit_bal_unadj_chained <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = NULL,
  data = balanced_panel, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "ipw",
  mode = "chained", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_bal_unadj_ordinary <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = NULL,
  data = balanced_panel, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "ipw",
  mode = "ordinary", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
unadj_comp <- merge(
  data.frame(group = fit_bal_unadj_chained$group, time = fit_bal_unadj_chained$t,
             chained = fit_bal_unadj_chained$att),
  data.frame(group = fit_bal_unadj_ordinary$group, time = fit_bal_unadj_ordinary$t,
             ordinary = fit_bal_unadj_ordinary$att),
  by = c("group", "time"), all = TRUE
)
max_abs_diff_unadj <- max(abs(unadj_comp$chained - unadj_comp$ordinary))
max_abs_diff_unadj
```

**What to inspect and try changing:**
- Read the printed `max_abs_diff_unadj` after matching cells by cohort and date: the telescoping reduction predicts agreement up to floating-point rounding, while both fits can share bias from omitting $X_i$. Point-estimate agreement alone also says nothing about equality of standard errors or bands.
- **Try changing:** Compare `fit_bal` (which uses `xformla = ~ x + z` and `est_method = "dr"`) against `mode = "ordinary"` with the same treatment method, formula, anticipation, and base period, matching cells by cohort and date. Inspect whether the pooled and separate regressions change the finite-sample estimates or standard errors.

## 10. Analytical Intervals, Multiplier Bands and Clustered Inference {#guide-10}

The earlier sections used analytical standard errors and pointwise normal intervals. Here `bstrap = TRUE` computes multiplier standard errors from the $N$-row study-unit influence functions; `cband = TRUE` requests a simultaneous band over available cells ([Uncertainty](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#uncertainty) and [Inference](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/inference.md)). The bootstrap does not refit the nuisance models. An exploratory `199` draws keeps this exercise manageable; increase the editable count for a more stable multiplier quantile. This is not a coverage experiment.

```{r}
#| label: multiplier-bands
bootstrap_draws <- 199L
set.seed(20261030)
fit_band <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = balanced_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying",
  bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE, biters = bootstrap_draws
)
knitr::kable(cdid::tidy(fit_band)[, c("target.id", "estimate", "std.error", "conf.low", "conf.high", "band.family")], digits = 4)
set.seed(20261031)
agg_band <- cdid::aggte(fit_band, type = "dynamic")
cdid::ggdid(agg_band)
agg_band$chained$overall[c("status", "inference_kind", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")]
```

Dynamic bins receive a simultaneous band; their scalar overall summary still has a pointwise interval. A simple aggregation also has a pointwise interval. Compare the cell estimates with `fit_bal`: the inference request changes uncertainty, not the fitted effects. Separate band families do not form a joint band over all outputs.

For genuinely correlated outcomes, draw a **separate** panel with nonzero cluster trend and request clustering. The generator records the cluster label for every study unit in `sim_cluster$units`. This example uses 100 independent clusters, rather than treating their study units as independent.

```{r}
#| label: clustered-inference
cfg_cluster <- cfg
cfg_cluster$seed <- 20261101L
cfg_cluster$n_clusters <- 100L
cfg_cluster$cluster_trend_sd <- 0.15
sim_cluster <- simulate_panel(cfg_cluster)
fit_cluster <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = sim_cluster$balanced_panel, frame = sim_cluster$units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying",
  clustervars = "cluster", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cdid::tidy(fit_cluster)[, c("target.id", "estimate", "std.error", "available")], digits = 4)
fit_cluster$chained$inference[c("kind", "clustered", "n_clusters", "n_total")]
```

**What to inspect and try changing:** Change `cfg_cluster$cluster_trend_sd` and redraw this separate study. Compare uncertainty only under an inference scheme appropriate for that DGP. For cluster multiplier bands, set `bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE, biters = bootstrap_draws` and set a seed before refitting. Large-sample approximations can be poor with few clusters; neither one draw nor a completed fit establishes nominal coverage.

## 11. Read Both Pretrend Tests and Their Availability {#guide-11}

`att_gt()` records a joint unconditional Wald test of **all** nonreference preperiod cells, without substituting an available subset ([Pretrend tests](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#pretrend-tests)). Read its full record alongside the cell table. Failure to reject is not evidence that parallel trends hold after treatment.

```{r}
#| label: unconditional-pretrend
list(W = fit_bal$W, Wpval = fit_bal$Wpval, record = fit_bal$chained$pretest)
knitr::kable(subset(cdid::tidy(fit_bal), role == "pre",
  select = c("target.id", "estimate", "std.error", "available")), digits = 4)
```

`conditional_did_pretest()` is a separate data-based call, not a method on `fit_bal`. It tests whether each preperiod comparison has zero conditional mean given the formula's design. Here `~ x` is sufficient: $Z_i$ is independent of treatment and observation given $X_i$, so its untreated trend averages to zero within each $X_i$/cohort group. The integration grid still uses the full study-unit table `units`; binary $X_i$ gives repeated design values and keeps the exercise simpler than a continuous grid. This call has no `pt_assumption`, `pt_start`, or GMM-weighting arguments.

```{r}
#| label: conditional-pretrend
set.seed(20261102)
pre_cond <- cdid::conditional_did_pretest(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x, selection_xformla = ~ x, data = missing_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", anticipation = 0,
  selection = "conditional_mtar", selection_est_method = "ipw",
  selection_model = "independent_period_logit", selection_pooling = "separate",
  selection_universe = "F", base_period = "varying",
  bstrap = TRUE, cband = TRUE, biters = bootstrap_draws
)
summary(pre_cond)
pre_cond[c("CvM", "CvMcval", "CvMpval")]
pre_cond$chained[c("status", "reason", "base_period")]
```

A separate illustration groups the **same balanced observations** into five clusters. Under the default cohorts, varying-base reports have six preperiod restrictions, while centered influence sums from five clusters have covariance rank at most four. The full Wald test is then unavailable; this is a test-covariance limitation, not a statement that ATT is unidentified. Five clusters also do not justify reliable large-sample inference ([Pretrend tests are unavailable](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/troubleshooting.md#pretrend-tests-are-unavailable)).

```{r}
#| label: few-cluster-pretrend
five_panel <- balanced_panel
five_units <- units
five_panel$cluster5 <- (five_panel$id - 1L) %% 5L + 1L
five_units$cluster5 <- (five_units$id - 1L) %% 5L + 1L
fit_five <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = five_panel, frame = five_units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", base_period = "varying",
  clustervars = "cluster5", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_five$chained$pretest
knitr::kable(cdid::tidy(fit_five)[, c("target.id", "estimate", "std.error", "available")], digits = 4)
```

**What to inspect and try changing:** Compare the two tests' recorded status and nulls. Change the five-cluster partition to more clusters and refit; read the actual full-test status instead of inventing a p-value or dropping restrictions. If you changed the main cohorts, the number of preperiod restrictions changes too.

## 12. Try the Treatment-DR Correctness Alternatives {#guide-12}

This exercise explores robustness when the treatment propensity $p$ or untreated change regression $m$ is misspecified separately. It draws three complete panels (`selection = "none"`, $N=1200$, $T=6$) with continuous $X_i \sim \text{Uniform}(-1,1)$. Unlike binary $X_i$, this allows a quadratic term that `~ x` cannot represent.

`xformla` supplies a **shared design for $p$ and $m$**; they cannot be set independently. Holding `xformla = ~ x` fixed, the datasets vary whether the true assignment log-odds or untreated trend includes $X_i^2$. All have cohort $G=3$ versus $G=0$ and effect $1+0.25(t-3)$ after treatment. The four posttreatment effects are $1.00,1.25,1.50,1.75$, giving the same simple ATT target, $1.375$.

The table gives the sufficient large-sample branches under parallel trends, no anticipation, overlap, valid GMM moments, and regularity conditions. See [Compare model robustness across treatment and missing outcome adjustments](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/robustness.md).

| Controlled case (`data`) | True DGP assignment log-odds | True DGP untreated per-period trend | Actual DGP model matched by `xformla = ~ x` | `est_method = "dr"` (uses $p$ and $m$) | `est_method = "reg"` / OR (uses $m$ only) | `est_method = "ipw"` (uses $p$ only) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `m_correct` (`rob_m`) | $0.6 X_i + 0.8 X_i^2$ | $0.4 + 0.3 X_i$ | $m$ correct; $p$ omits $X_i^2$ | Consistent (via correct $m$) | Consistent (via correct $m$) | No consistency guarantee ($p$ misspecified) |
| `p_correct` (`rob_p`) | $0.6 X_i$ | $0.4 + 0.3 X_i^2$ | $p$ correct; $m$ omits $X_i^2$ | Consistent (via correct $p$) | No consistency guarantee ($m$ misspecified) | Consistent (via correct $p$) |
| `both_wrong` (`rob_both`) | $0.6 X_i + 0.8 X_i^2$ | $0.4 + 0.3 X_i^2$ | Neither ($p$ and $m$ both omit $X_i^2$) | No consistency guarantee | No consistency guarantee | No consistency guarantee |

“No consistency guarantee” does not mean an estimator must fail. In `p_correct`, symmetry and $P(G=3\mid X)=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(0.6X)$ give $E[X^2\mid G=3]=E[X^2\mid G=0]$, even though linear $m$ cannot represent the quadratic conditional trend. Moment or projection cancellations can matter. Even `both_wrong` may be near truth in one draw; closeness alone does not establish consistency, bias, coverage, or efficiency.

The original-target branches also require inactive probability safeguards in the population or additional target-preserving conditions; ordinary IF inference needs negligible threshold-crossing remainder. True propensities here are bounded away from zero and one, but fitted models still need regular limits. The package caps treatment propensities at $1-10^{-6}$ and floors inverse observation denominators at $10^{-6}$ ([Probability safeguards](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/missing-outcomes.md#probability-safeguards)).

Treatment DR supplies the $p$-or-$m$ branch only. With missing outcomes it gives no general protection against an incorrect $q$ or $j$; see [Section 8](#guide-8) and [Correctness conditions across both layers](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/examples/robustness.md#correctness-conditions-across-both-layers).

```{r}
#| label: robustness-draw
set.seed(20261103)
n_robust <- 1200L
x_robust <- stats::runif(n_robust, -1, 1)
u_robust <- stats::runif(n_robust)
g_linear <- ifelse(u_robust < stats::plogis(0.6 * x_robust), 3L, 0L)
g_curved <- ifelse(u_robust < stats::plogis(0.6 * x_robust + 0.8 * x_robust^2), 3L, 0L)
robust_base <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(n_robust), each = 6L),
  time = rep(1:6, n_robust), x = rep(x_robust, each = 6L))
robust_noise <- rep(stats::rnorm(n_robust), each = 6L) +
  stats::rnorm(nrow(robust_base), sd = 0.5)
rob_m <- rob_p <- rob_both <- robust_base
rob_m$g <- rob_both$g <- rep(g_curved, each = 6L)
rob_p$g <- rep(g_linear, each = 6L)
rob_m$y <- robust_noise + (0.4 + 0.3 * rob_m$x) * rob_m$time +
  ifelse(rob_m$g > 0 & rob_m$time >= 3, 1 + 0.25 * (rob_m$time - 3), 0)
rob_p$y <- robust_noise + (0.4 + 0.3 * rob_p$x^2) * rob_p$time +
  ifelse(rob_p$g > 0 & rob_p$time >= 3, 1 + 0.25 * (rob_p$time - 3), 0)
rob_both$y <- robust_noise + (0.4 + 0.3 * rob_both$x^2) * rob_both$time +
  ifelse(rob_both$g > 0 & rob_both$time >= 3, 1 + 0.25 * (rob_both$time - 3), 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: robustness-dr-fits
fit_rob_m <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = ~ x,
  data = rob_m, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "none", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_rob_p <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = ~ x,
  data = rob_p, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "none", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_rob_both <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = ~ x,
  data = rob_both, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr",
  selection = "none", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
rob_agg <- list(m_correct = cdid::aggte(fit_rob_m, type = "simple"),
  p_correct = cdid::aggte(fit_rob_p, type = "simple"),
  both_wrong = cdid::aggte(fit_rob_both, type = "simple"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(case = names(rob_agg),
  estimate = vapply(rob_agg, function(a) a$overall.att, numeric(1)),
  std.error = vapply(rob_agg, function(a) a$overall.se, numeric(1)),
  population_att = 1.375), digits = 6,
  caption = "Doubly robust (est_method = 'dr') simple ATT estimates across the three continuous-X correctness cases")
```

To compare the single-model alternatives (`est_method = "reg"` for OR and `est_method = "ipw"` for IPW) directly against `est_method = "dr"` on these **same three predeclared draws** (`rob_m`, `rob_p`, `rob_both`), run the opt-in chunk below interactively (excluded from automatic rendering to keep default notebook render times light):

```{r}
#| label: optional-robustness-ipw-reg-comparison
#| eval: false
rob_cases <- list(m_correct = rob_m, p_correct = rob_p, both_wrong = rob_both)
rob_method_grid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rob_cases), function(case_name) {
  d <- rob_cases[[case_name]]
  fit_or <- cdid::att_gt(
    yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = ~ x,
    data = d, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "reg",
    selection = "none", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
  )
  fit_ipw <- cdid::att_gt(
    yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g", xformla = ~ x,
    data = d, control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "ipw",
    selection = "none", pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
  )
  agg_dr  <- rob_agg[[case_name]]
  agg_or  <- cdid::aggte(fit_or, type = "simple")
  agg_ipw <- cdid::aggte(fit_ipw, type = "simple")
  data.frame(
    case           = case_name,
    est_method     = c("dr", "reg", "ipw"),
    simple_att     = c(agg_dr$overall.att, agg_or$overall.att, agg_ipw$overall.att),
    std_error      = c(agg_dr$overall.se, agg_or$overall.se, agg_ipw$overall.se),
    population_att = 1.375,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(rob_method_grid, digits = 6,
             caption = "Comparison of dr, reg (OR), and ipw across m_correct, p_correct, and both_wrong on the same draws")
```

**What to inspect and try changing:** Compare each estimate and SE with the target `1.375` and the expected branches in the table. The enabled chunk fits DR only; the disabled chunk adds OR/IPW on the same draws. To make both models representable in all three cases, try `xformla = ~ x + I(x^2)` in the calls. Rebuild aggregates after refitting, and keep failures visible.

## 13. Dated Covariates and Explicit Weight Anchors {#guide-13}

Covariates can vary within a study unit. For posttreatment comparisons of cohort $g$, `cdid` reads each study unit's covariates at that cohort's reference date; preperiod reports read them at the earlier endpoint. Required values come from dated rows even when their outcomes are missing. Keep those rows and do not put a conflicting static version in `frame`.

This recipe uses the complete outcomes to isolate reference inputs. `x_date = x + 0.05*time` is a known shift of the original $X_i$ at each anchor, so the original linear treatment and trend specifications remain representable. Changing weights require an explicit `fix_weights`: `"first_period"` uses each study unit's first-calendar weight throughout; `"base_period"` uses its weight at the target cohort's reference date, including for controls.

```{r}
#| label: dated-inputs-and-weights
dated_panel <- balanced_panel
dated_panel$x_date <- dated_panel$x + 0.05 * dated_panel$time
dated_panel$w_date <- exp(0.15 * dated_panel$x * dated_panel$time)
dated_frame <- units[, c("id", "g")]
head(dated_panel[dated_panel$time %in% c(2, 3, 4),
                 c("id", "time", "g", "y", "x_date", "z", "w_date")])
fit_weight_first <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x_date + z, data = dated_panel, frame = dated_frame,
  weightsname = "w_date", fix_weights = "first_period",
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
fit_weight_base <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x_date + z, data = dated_panel, frame = dated_frame,
  weightsname = "w_date", fix_weights = "base_period",
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
weight_first <- cdid::aggte(fit_weight_first, type = "simple")
weight_base <- cdid::aggte(fit_weight_base, type = "simple")
knitr::kable(data.frame(anchor = c("first_period", "base_period"),
  estimate = c(weight_first$overall.att, weight_base$overall.att),
  std.error = c(weight_first$overall.se, weight_base$overall.se)), digits = 4)
```

Both targets are weighted, so the core's unweighted `sim$truth` is not their benchmark. With base-period anchoring, cohort cells have different reference weight laws; aggregation is a declared mixture using first-calendar cohort masses, not a single common weighted population. If weights are constant within each study unit, the anchor choices coincide. See [reference inputs](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/prepare-data.md) and [Changing covariates and weights](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/options.md).

**What to inspect and try changing:** Set `w_date <- exp(0.15 * dated_panel$x)` and refit both calls to compare fixed weights. To use missing outcomes instead, keep required covariate/weight reference rows with `y = NA` and choose a valid missing-outcome adjustment from [Sections 5–8](#guide-5); a missing outcome is never a zero.

## 14. GMM Weighting, Diagnostics and Point-Only Fits {#guide-14}

`gmm_weighting = "optimal"` (also named `"two_step"`) requests feasible two-step GMM; the core used this default. `"identity"` explicitly requests the unweighted full-catalog criterion. Under optimal weighting, automatic Tikhonov regularization can stabilize a singular or poorly conditioned comparison covariance after exact structural reductions. It cannot supply missing ATT identification. Read the actual record rather than assuming regularization occurred.

```{r}
#| label: gmm-and-resources
workspace_bytes <- 1073741824  # Counted numeric-array workspace, 1 GiB.
work_cap <- Inf               # No estimated work cap; choose a finite whole number to opt in.
fit_identity <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = balanced_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE,
  gmm_weighting = "identity", gmm_covariance = "tikhonov",
  control = list(numeric_workspace_bytes = workspace_bytes, counted_work_limit = work_cap)
)
list(optimal = fit_bal$chained$covariance_handling[c("weighting_requested", "weighting_canonical",
       "handler_invoked", "handler_used", "trigger_reason", "lambda")],
     optimal_conditioning = fit_bal$chained$covariance_handling$conditioning[c("rho", "d_min", "d_max")],
     identity = fit_identity$chained$covariance_handling[c("weighting_requested", "weighting_canonical",
       "handler_invoked", "handler_used", "trigger_reason", "lambda")])
fit_identity$chained$public[c("counted_work_limit", "work_cap")]
```

Workspace and estimated work limits do not cap total process memory or elapsed time. `print_details = TRUE` provides progress messages; `chunk_rows` can be set in `control` when needed. Too little workspace or a binding work cap produces a refusal, with no automatic estimator substitution. Probability safeguards cap fitted treatment propensities at `1 - 1e-6` and floor inverse observation denominators at `1e-6`; they do not rescue separation, deficient rank, or unsupported predictions. See [diagnosing failures](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/help/troubleshooting.md) and [GMM](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/methods/gmm.md).

For point estimates alone, turn off influence-function computation. This fit has no standard errors, pretrend test, or subsequent aggregation ([Point estimates only](https://github.com/dvbn/cdid/blob/main/docs/reference/results.md#point-estimates-only)).

```{r}
#| label: point-only
fit_point <- cdid::att_gt(
  yname = "y", tname = "time", idname = "id", gname = "g",
  xformla = ~ x + z, data = balanced_panel, frame = units,
  control_group = "nevertreated", est_method = "dr", selection = "none",
  pt_assumption = "post", compute_inffunc = FALSE, bstrap = FALSE, cband = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(cdid::tidy(fit_point)[, c("target.id", "estimate", "std.error", "available")], digits = 4)
fit_point$chained$inference$kind
```

The next chunk is deliberately **not run when rendering**. Run it manually only to see the documented refusal: `aggte()` requires stored influence functions. It is an expected API restriction, not a catch-all for an unexpected fitting failure.

```{r}
#| label: expected-point-only-refusal
#| eval: false
cdid::aggte(fit_point, type = "simple")
```

**What to inspect and try changing:** Compare `fit_point`'s estimates with `fit_bal` by cohort and date.
